amendments.rule:
An inflected verb may align to an English subject pronoun, auxiliary, and main verb together. Choose the lexical English verb as the target head. **This permission is specific to a pronoun realizing the verb's person and number.** A lexical English subject noun the ASV supplies where no source nominal is present answers to no morpheme and is its own `added` unit: `יָשְׁבוּ בָהּ` → *men shall dwell therein* gives *shall dwell* to the verb and leaves *men* `added`. **A volitive English frame belongs to the verb whose mood it renders.** Where the ASV expands an imperative or jussive with *Oh* or *Oh that ... would*, the framing words join the verb's unit and the unit heads on its lexical predicate: `הוֹדוּ` → *Oh give thanks* heads on *thanks* under rule 44, and `יוֹדוּ` → *Oh that ... would praise* heads on *praise*. A lexical subject noun supplied inside that frame is still `added` under the preceding sentence — *Oh that men would praise* leaves *men* outside the verb's discontinuous unit. This applies only where no optative particle or multi-source optative idiom stands in the Hebrew; a present `לוּ` or `מִי יִתֵּן` takes its own fixed English formula under rule 30. **A presentative dummy *there* is not such a lexical subject.** Where the ASV recasts a finite verb or participle with a presentative frame — `יֵּצֵא` → *there came forth*, `נִשֵּׂאת` → *there was lifted up* — the dummy belongs to the verb's unit, by the same constructional reasoning that puts it on `הָיָה` under rule 21, and the unit still heads on the lexical verb. When the verse also has an explicit subject noun, that noun's tokens are its own unit and only a genuinely pleonastic pronoun stays with the verb. **Where the ASV recasts a waw plus an explicit subject pronoun as a relative clause, the English *who* or *which* realizes the pronoun; the waw is `unrepresented` if the ASV writes no separate connective.** Do not give the relative pronoun to the waw merely because it opens the recast clause: `וְהוּא אַחֲרָיו` → *which was behind him* gives *which* to `הוּא` and leaves the waw unrepresented, and `וַאֲנִי זָקַנְתִּי` → *who am old* gives *who* to `אֲנִי` on the same terms. **A question auxiliary the ASV fronts belongs to the interrogative particle and not to the verb.** English marks a yes-or-no question by fronting an auxiliary, and where `הֲ` stands in the clause that word is what the ASV has written for it: `הֲלוֹא לֶאֱמוּנָה` → *do not thine eyes look upon truth* gives *do* to `הֲ` in a clause that has no verb at all to take it, and `הַעַל אֵלֶּה לֹא אֶפְקֹד` → *Shall I not visit* gives *Shall* to `הֲ` and *I visit* to the verb, even though that auxiliary also carries the imperfect's future. The `אִם` opening a following disjunctive question is read the same way, since it is what marks that clause as the second question: `אִם לֹא תָחִילוּ` → *will ye not tremble* gives *will* to `אִם` and *ye tremble* to the verb. **But a particle for which the ASV has written a connective of its own is not a home for the auxiliary as well.** Where the ASV renders that `אִם`, or another particle standing at the head of the second question, by a written *Or*, *Or if* or another connective, that word is the particle's under rule 14, the particle takes no second English word, and the fronted auxiliary is the ordinary one this rule's first sentence gives the verb: `אִם יְדַבֵּר אֵלֶיךָ רַכּוֹת` → ***Or*** *will he speak soft words unto thee* gives *Or* to `אִם` and *will he speak* to the verb. This is the reasoning of this rule's second limit below, where an interrogative holding an English word of its own leaves the auxiliary to the verb, and of rule 51's ruling that a waw holding a connective of its own is not a home for a second word. Count the clause's English function words against the morphemes that could carry them, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s; where the ASV writes no connective for the particle, the preceding sentence governs as before. Where the ASV marks the question by inversion alone and writes no auxiliary, the particle is `unrepresented`: `הַאוֹתִי לֹא תִירָאוּ` → *Fear ye not me*. Two limits. Where no interrogative morpheme is present at all, a fronted *do* is the verb's own under this rule's first sentence: `לֹא שָׁפָטוּ` → *do they not judge*. And this governs the yes-or-no particle only: an interrogative word that has an English word of its own — `מָה` → *what*, `אֵי` → *How* — leaves the fronted auxiliary to the verb, as `אֵי לָזֹאת אֶסְלַח לָךְ` → *How can I pardon thee* leaves *can I pardon* whole.

**An English matrix duration frame is not an auxiliary of the finite verb inside the temporal clause it introduces.** Where `עַד` plus a temporal interrogative and `לֹא` plus a finite verb is rendered *how long will it be ere ...*, the temporal-interrogative expression takes *how long will it be* as one `noncompositional` unit, headed on *long*; the negative takes *ere*; and the finite verb takes only its subordinate subject and predicate. `עַד מָתַי לֹא יוּכְלוּ` → *how long will it be ere they attain* and `עַד אָנָה לֹא תִשְׁקֹטִי` → *how long will it be ere thou be quiet* follow that division. The dummy *it* is not the finite verb's person and number, and assigning the matrix frame to that verb would give it two English clauses. This does not make a simple *how long ...* indivisible where the ASV writes no separate matrix frame; there each morpheme is aligned on its own merits under rule 2.

**Where the ASV recasts a waw plus a finite verb as a relative clause and no explicit subject pronoun stands in that clause, the relative *who* or *which* is the connective the ASV has written for the waw and belongs to the waw; the verb keeps its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb.** `וַתֹּאכַל` → *which hath devoured* gives *which* to the waw and *hath devoured* to the verb. This is the other side of the explicit-pronoun case above: a present pronoun takes the relative before the waw does, but without one the waw is the morpheme licensing the relative connective. Where no waw or other conjunction stands either, rule 55 governs the supplied relative instead. The finished corpus aligns a waw directly to *which* in ten units, so this is settled rather than a tie to hedge.
amendments.why: JOB.41.3 writes `אִם` at the head of the second of two disjunctive questions and the ASV renders it *Or will he speak soft words unto thee*. Rule 17's `אִם` sentence, written for `אִם לֹא תָחִילוּ` → *will ye not tremble* where the ASV writes no connective, would hand *will* to the particle; rule 14 independently claims the written *Or* for it, and the two together would give one morpheme both words while leaving the verb's ordinary imperfect auxiliary unaccounted for. The contract already resolves this shape everywhere else — this rule's own second limit leaves the auxiliary to the verb where `מָה` or `אֵי` holds a word of its own, rule 51 says a waw holding a connective of its own is not a home for a second one, and rules 43 and 52 run the same count for prepositions and suffixes — so the amendment states that settled counting for the yes-or-no and disjunctive particles rather than making a new claim, and it leaves rule 17's unrendered-connective example untouched. The verse pass reached this reading and named the competing one; recording it as a qualification of rule 17 keeps the over-broad sentence from being read on its own by the next chapter that meets an `אִם` with a written *Or*.

conventions: Where the ASV renders one comparative preposition by an elliptical or correlative English expression, the whole expression is that preposition's single rendering under rule 30 and no part of it is `added` or handed to the noun or predicate beside it: כַּ → 'as with' (41.5), כְּ → 'As of' (41.20), and כְּמוֹ → 'as ... as' (41.24), the last discontinuous around the predicate participle under rule 25 and headed on the occurrence governing the noun. The competing reading, which marks the second English word `added`, was live in 41.5 and 41.20 and was declined because no other morpheme stands for it. This does not reach a degree word the ASV writes with no comparative preposition in the clause: the 'so' of 41.10 and 41.16 belongs to the predicate it modifies.

A supplied English attributive standing beside a Hebrew noun joins that noun's unit under rule 31 where it elaborates the noun's own lexeme — 'burning torches' for לַפִּידִים (41.19), 'the pointed shaft' for שִׁרְיָה (41.26), 'the bands of fishermen' for חַבָּרִים (41.6), 'a pot of ointment' for מֶרְקָחָה (41.31) — and is its own `added` unit under rule 20's supplied-lexical-verb boundary where it instead predicates of the noun something the Hebrew does not write and the noun's own rendering is already complete: the italic 'burning' before 'rushes' in 41.20, where אַגְמֹן is fully rendered by 'rushes' and the coordination's one participle נָפוּחַ has already been spent on 'boiling'. Ask which of the two the English word is doing before folding it in; the ASV's italic corroborates either way and decides neither (rule 7).

report: Checked all 27 candidate lemma groups. Every printed difference is the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in different contexts, not one construction analysed two ways: בְּ (into/with/to/In), לְ (for/as/at/into/to be), מִן (Out of/from/When/By reason of), עַל (of/upon/over) and כְּ (as/like/as with/As of/are like) each take the word the ASV wrote for them, and the pronominal-suffix groups differ only as possessive against object.

Interrogatives are consistent and the difference is licensed by the source: הֲ/הַ takes the fronted auxiliary in 41.2, 41.3, 41.4, 41.5, 41.7 and 41.9; 41.1 writes no interrogative morpheme at all, so 'Canst' is the verb's own under rule 17's first limit. 41.3's אִם holds the written 'Or' and leaves 'will' to the verb — the one place the chapter had to choose between rule 17's אִם sentence and rule 14, and the basis of the amendment below.

Read the dump end to end for the 13 added units, since the candidate table is blind to them. The connective count runs correctly in both directions: supplied 'and'/'And' added where no waw stands (41.8, 41.19, 41.27), the waw unrepresented where the ASV opens bare (41.29), written waws on written connectives elsewhere; supplied subordinators 'That' (41.4) and 'If' (41.26) added against the waw-borne 'That' (41.16) and 'so that' (41.17); supplied possessives added where no suffix stands (41.12, 41.15 twice) against the fifteen suffix-borne possessives.

Verb-reaching prepositions are consistent: 'of him' (41.6) goes to the written עַל, while 'unto me' (41.11), 'concerning his limbs' (41.12) and 'at him' (41.26) go to the verb because no preposition morpheme stands there — rule 44's limit applied in both directions. Copula placement (41.11, 41.14, 41.15, 41.18, 41.24, 41.30, 41.34) always lands on the clause's predicate word, with 41.14's competing reading named in that verse.

Nearest thing to a split: 41.19 folds the supplied 'burning' into לַפִּידִים under rule 31, while 41.20 marks 'burning' added. Judged licensed — the first elaborates the noun's own lexeme, the second predicates an event of a noun whose rendering is already complete, which is rule 20's boundary — and recorded as a convention rather than patched.

BSB: the single disagreement (41.17, the suffix of אָחִיהוּ) is the documented convention difference and not an error. The ASV writes 'one to another' with no pronoun and 'another' carries no possessive, so nothing realizes the suffix; the chapter reads the parallel אֶחָד בְּאֶחָד of 41.16 the same way. No accepted edge was changed to move the aggregate.

Also checked and found uniform, so not logged as conventions because the contract already decides them: 'cannot' goes whole to whatever negative stands in the clause (לֹא 41.17 and 41.28, בַּל 41.23, בְּלִי 41.26), with the verb keeping its subject and auxiliary discontinuously and no יָכֹל anywhere in the chapter; and the impersonal English 'one' (41.9, 41.26, 41.32) stays with its verb as a pronoun realizing its person and number, not as rule 17's supplied lexical subject noun.
